meaning: a regular, customary way of doing things in a fixed order
examples: I follow a calm morning routine before going to university.
Reading books every night is an essential part of her bedtime routine.
memoryTip: Think of 'route' — a familiar path you travel along every single day.

meaning: a short journey made to deliver or collect something or complete a chore
examples: I have a quick errand to run at the post office before lunch.
She spent Saturday morning running grocery errands for her grandparents.
memoryTip: Rhymes with 'end' — you go out with a purpose and bring it to a quick end.

meaning: routine domestic tasks such as cleaning, washing, or tidying
examples: The children share household chores like washing dishes and taking out the bins.
Finishing my chores early leaves the entire afternoon free for relaxation.
memoryTip: Sounds like 'bore' — chores are everyday tasks that may feel repetitive but keep life orderly.

meaning: a person living next door or near to you
examples: Our friendly neighbor watered our garden while we were away on holiday.
Living in a close-knit neighborhood means everyone knows their neighbors.
memoryTip: Contains 'near' — someone who dwells near your doorstep.

meaning: a plan that gives expected times for different events or activities
examples: Her tight lecture schedule leaves very little time for midday breaks.
The train arrived right on schedule despite the heavy rainfall.
memoryTip: Picture your school timetable — a schedule keeps your week on track.

meaning: fitting in well with a person's needs, activities, or easy to reach
examples: Having a grocery store right across the street is incredibly convenient.
Please contact me whenever it is most convenient for you.
memoryTip: Think of a 'convenience store' — open 24/7 because it saves you time and effort.

meaning: to arrange things systematically or coordinate an event
examples: She took an hour to organize her study desk and file her notes.
The student council helped organize a welcoming party for freshmen.
memoryTip: Think of body 'organs' — each has a specific, orderly place and purpose.

meaning: to make something ready for use or make oneself ready for an event
examples: He woke up early to prepare a nutritious breakfast for his family.
Students should prepare thoroughly before sitting for their semester exams.
memoryTip: Prefix 'pre-' means before — getting things set before action begins.

meaning: to take and use something belonging to someone else with the intention of returning it
examples: Can I borrow your umbrella until tomorrow afternoon?
Students often borrow academic journals from the campus library.
memoryTip: Borrow means taking, while lend means giving — remember 'B' comes before 'L'.

meaning: to restore something broken, damaged, or torn to good condition
examples: The technician arrived within an hour to repair the leaking washing machine.
It took several weeks of calm communication to repair their friendship.
memoryTip: To 're-pair' is to put two broken pieces back together as a working pair.

meaning: an estimate of income and expenditure for a set period of time
examples: Living within a monthly budget helps students save money for emergencies.
The renovation project was completed on time and well within budget.
memoryTip: A budget guards your pocket so your expenses don't budge out of control.

meaning: a device or piece of equipment designed to perform a specific household task
examples: Modern kitchen appliances like dishwashers and microwaves save valuable time.
Remember to unplug heavy appliances before going away on long trips.
memoryTip: You 'apply' it to a household chore to get the work done quickly.

meaning: a state in which one is not observed or disturbed by other people
examples: She closed the bedroom door so she could study in complete privacy.
Digital security settings allow you to protect your personal privacy online.
memoryTip: Connects directly with 'private' — your own protected personal space.

meaning: the process of keeping something in good condition through routine care
examples: Regular vehicle maintenance prevents sudden breakdowns and costly repairs.
The apartment building underwent roof maintenance throughout the spring.
memoryTip: Think of 'maintain' — routine care that maintains strength and performance.

meaning: consistently good in quality or performance, and able to be trusted
examples: Public transport in this city is remarkably reliable and always on time.
He proved to be a reliable partner who delivered on every single promise.
memoryTip: Someone you can 'rely' on is 'rely-able'.

meaning: achieving maximum productivity with minimum wasted effort or expense
examples: Using keyboard shortcuts makes drafting documents much more efficient.
An energy-efficient air conditioner lowered our electricity bills significantly.
memoryTip: Efficiency turns effort into effect without wasting energy.

meaning: to arrange or treat things in order of importance
examples: During exam weeks, it is crucial to prioritize sleep alongside revision.
Busy managers learn to prioritize urgent assignments over minor requests.
memoryTip: Putting what is 'prior' (first in importance) at the top of your list.

meaning: to distribute resources or duties for a specific purpose
examples: I allocate forty-five minutes every evening strictly to reading literature.
The city council decided to allocate extra funds for public park repairs.
memoryTip: Think of locating a spot ('locate') to set aside funds or time.

meaning: to discuss something formally with others in order to reach an agreement
examples: The tenants met with the landlord to negotiate a fair lease extension.
She managed to negotiate a lower price when buying the antique dining table.
memoryTip: When you negotiate, you exchange dialogue until both sides say 'yes'.

meaning: one of two or more available possibilities or options
examples: Cycling to campus is a healthier alternative to sitting in crowded buses.
When the highway was closed, drivers searched for a scenic alternative route.
memoryTip: From 'alter' (to change) — an alternate route that changes your direction.

meaning: to delay or postpone doing something that must be done, usually through laziness or distraction
examples: If you procrastinate on your final project, the deadline will cause undue panic.
He tends to procrastinate by cleaning his entire apartment instead of writing his paper.
memoryTip: From Latin 'cras' (tomorrow) — putting things off until tomorrow and tomorrow.

meaning: having the ability to find quick, clever ways to overcome difficulties
examples: A resourceful cook can create a delicious dinner from whatever leftovers are in the fridge.
She proved resourceful during the power outage by converting phone torches into soft room lanterns.
memoryTip: Full of resources — even when tools are scarce, your mind finds the solution.

meaning: showing great attention to detail, very careful and precise
examples: Her meticulous organization of our shared files made finding documents effortless.
The tailor took meticulous measurements to ensure the suit fitted flawlessly.
memoryTip: Meticulous people tick off every detail like a ticking clock.

meaning: an agreement or settlement reached by each side making concessions
examples: Finding a good compromise over household chores kept the flatmates on great terms.
After hours of debate, both sides reached a sensible compromise on the budget.
memoryTip: Both promise to meet halfway — 'co-promise'.

meaning: the capacity to recover quickly from difficulties; toughness and bounce-back ability
examples: Her emotional resilience carried her through a difficult first year at university.
The community showed extraordinary resilience as they rebuilt their town after the storm.
memoryTip: Like a spring that bounces back into shape after being squeezed.

meaning: a period of learning or teaching about a particular subject
examples: Our chemistry professor began the lesson with a captivating demonstration.
Making mistakes in your first draft teaches you an invaluable writing lesson.
memoryTip: Take a lesson to lessen your confusion on a difficult topic.

meaning: a person who is studying at a school, college, or university
examples: Every student in the seminar was encouraged to share their perspective.
As a lifelong student of history, he spends his weekends browsing archives.
memoryTip: Someone who dedicates time to study — 'study-ant'.

meaning: a branch of knowledge studied or taught in an educational institution
examples: Mathematics has always been her strongest academic subject.
The lecture covered a fascinating subject that sparked a long debate.
memoryTip: The main topic that your study is subjected to.

meaning: a sentence worded or expressed so as to elicit information
examples: The lecturer paused after each slide to invite questions from the audience.
Asking insightful questions is one of the best ways to deepen your understanding.
memoryTip: A 'quest' for information — asking a question starts the journey of learning.

meaning: a thing said, written, or done to deal with or satisfy a question or problem
examples: She raised her hand immediately because she knew the correct answer.
There is rarely a single simple answer to complex economic challenges.
memoryTip: An answer serves as the anchor that settles a question.

meaning: repeated exercise in an activity or skill so as to acquire or maintain proficiency
examples: Regular coding practice is the fastest route to software development mastery.
With twenty minutes of vocabulary practice each day, your fluency will surge.
memoryTip: Practice makes progress — repeating a skill locks it into muscle memory.

meaning: to make an idea or situation clear to someone by describing it in more detail
examples: Could you please explain how you arrived at this formula in your calculation?
The textbook uses real-world diagrams to explain how photosynthesis operates.
memoryTip: Make it plain — 'ex-plain' turns complicated concepts into plain English.

meaning: the systematic investigation into and study of materials and sources to establish facts
examples: Her groundbreaking cancer research was published in an international medical journal.
Students must conduct thorough primary research before drafting their dissertations.
memoryTip: To 're-search' — looking deeply again and again until truth is uncovered.

meaning: to examine or study again especially as a means of correction or revision
examples: Take thirty minutes every Sunday to review the notes you gathered during the week.
The admissions committee will carefully review each candidate's application portfolio.
memoryTip: To 're-view' literally means to view something a second time with fresh eyes.

meaning: eager to know or learn something new
examples: The young scientist was always curious about how celestial bodies form in space.
A curious mindset turns everyday challenges into exciting learning opportunities.
memoryTip: Curiosity cured boredom — eager questions ignite curiosity.

meaning: to make or become better in quality, value, or capability
examples: Practicing vocabulary flashcards every morning will steadily improve your test score.
Constructive feedback from your tutor will help you improve your essay structure.
memoryTip: To prove yourself in a skill by upgrading it step by step.

meaning: to focus all one's attention or mental effort on a particular object or activity
examples: I find it much easier to concentrate in the quiet study zones of the library.
Turn off smartphone notifications when you need to concentrate on difficult assignments.
memoryTip: Bring all your thoughts together into one single 'center'.

meaning: a task or piece of work allocated to someone as part of a course of study or job
examples: Our professor uploaded the semester project assignment to the student portal today.
She completed her programming assignment well before the midnight deadline.
memoryTip: A duty 'assigned' to you by a teacher or supervisor.

meaning: a source of supply, support, or information that can be readily drawn upon
examples: The university digital archive is an invaluable resource for graduate researchers.
Effective teachers share online resources that guide independent student learning.
memoryTip: Re-source — going back to the source where knowledge flows.

meaning: relating to education and scholarship at schools, colleges, and universities
examples: She received an academic scholarship based on her remarkable entrance exam scores.
Writing clear academic papers requires disciplined research and formal vocabulary.
memoryTip: Trace back to the ancient Greek 'Academy' founded by Plato for learning.

meaning: to form an idea of the amount, number, or value of; assess
examples: Teachers use rubrics to evaluate student presentations objectively and fairly.
Take time to evaluate your study habits and identify where you lose focus.
memoryTip: Notice 'value' inside 'evaluate' — determining the true value of work.

meaning: correct in all details; free from error
examples: Scientific experiments rely on accurate measurements taken with calibrated tools.
An accurate citation list ensures your research papers respect academic integrity.
memoryTip: Hit the bullseye with 'accuracy' — right on the mark with zero mistakes.

meaning: to explain or understand the meaning of information, words, or actions
examples: Literature students learn how to interpret subtle metaphors in classical poetry.
The statistical analyst had to interpret contradictory survey findings for the board.
memoryTip: An interpreter bridges the gap between foreign languages and understanding.

meaning: an abstract idea or a general notion conceived in the mind
examples: Gravity is a fundamental physical concept that explains planetary orbits.
Once you grasp the core concept of object-oriented programming, coding feels natural.
memoryTip: Conceived in the mind — a concept is a mental blueprint for understanding.

meaning: a detailed examination of the elements or structure of something
examples: Her in-depth data analysis revealed surprising consumer behavior trends.
The thesis opens with a comparative analysis of two twentieth-century novels.
memoryTip: Breaks a complex whole into pieces so each piece can be understood.

meaning: to grasp mentally; understand fully
examples: The reading comprehension section tests whether students truly comprehend the passages.
He struggled to comprehend the full philosophical depth of the ancient text.
memoryTip: Latin 'prehendere' means to seize — your mind seizes and holds the idea.

meaning: a principle or standard by which something may be judged or decided
examples: Originality of thought is a decisive criterion when evaluating graduate essays.
The scholarship committee uses academic excellence as its primary selection criterion.
memoryTip: Critique uses criteria — a criterion is the rule a critic uses to judge.

meaning: including or dealing with all or nearly all elements or aspects of something
examples: The syllabus provides a comprehensive overview of modern European history.
She conducted a comprehensive review of all medical trials published in the decade.
memoryTip: It comprehends everything — leaving no stone unturned in coverage.

meaning: to combine a number of things into a coherent, unified whole
examples: A great literature review must synthesize multiple research papers into one coherent narrative.
The researcher was able to synthesize data from twelve countries into a predictive model.
memoryTip: Prefix 'syn-' means together (like synergy) — bringing diverse parts together.

meaning: a high degree of competence or skill; expertise
examples: Demonstrating English language proficiency is required for international degree programs.
Years of dedicated studio practice elevated his piano proficiency to concert standards.
memoryTip: A 'professional' possesses high 'proficiency' in their craft.

meaning: a person or organization that buys goods or services from a store or business
examples: Providing polite and swift assistance keeps every customer satisfied and loyal.
The online bookstore launched a loyalty rewards program for returning customers.
memoryTip: It's their custom (habit) to purchase from your store.

meaning: an assembly of people for discussion, especially in a business or professional context
examples: The engineering team scheduled a daily standup meeting to track sprint progress.
Minutes of the board meeting were circulated to all executive directors.
memoryTip: A place where minds 'meet' to make decisions.

meaning: an article or substance that is manufactured or refined for sale
examples: The startup designed an eco-friendly cleaning product packaged in recycled glass.
User testing helped the designers refine the software product before public release.
memoryTip: What you produce to sell on the market.

meaning: a financial gain, especially the difference between amount earned and cost of buying or producing
examples: The café recorded a healthy annual profit after reducing food waste.
They reinvested fifty percent of their net profits into research and development.
memoryTip: Revenue minus expenses leaves you with the profit in your pocket.

meaning: a person or organization that employs people and pays them wages
examples: A progressive employer provides comprehensive healthcare and flexible working hours.
The tech company is recognized as one of the country's top graduate employers.
memoryTip: The employer hires, whereas the employee is hired.

meaning: an occupation undertaken for a significant period of a person's life with opportunities for progress
examples: She built an illustrious thirty-year career in international commercial law.
University internships give undergraduates early insights into prospective careers.
memoryTip: Think of a road or career track you travel along across your working life.

meaning: to start or set in motion an activity, enterprise, or systematically release a product
examples: The studio plans to launch their new educational mobile app next month.
They held a press conference in Tokyo to launch the global marketing campaign.
memoryTip: Like launching a rocket into space — propelling a new venture out into the world.

meaning: to expend money with the expectation of achieving a profit or material result
examples: Angel venture funds often invest in promising early-stage clean-energy startups.
It is wise to invest time in mastering English vocabulary while you are still at university.
memoryTip: Putting resources 'in' today so value grows in the future.

meaning: to be in charge of a business, project, or group of staff; administer and regulate
examples: She was promoted to manage a multidisciplinary team of twelve software engineers.
Learning to manage cash flow effectively determines whether a small business survives.
memoryTip: Having your hands ('manus' in Latin) on the wheel to guide operations.

meaning: a written or spoken agreement, especially one concerning employment, sales, or tenancy, enforceable by law
examples: Both companies signed a five-year contract to supply solar panels across the region.
Make sure you consult a qualified legal advisor before signing any binding contract.
memoryTip: Draws parties 'together' (con-) into a legal commitment.

meaning: the total amount of income generated by the sale of goods or services related to operations
examples: Quarterly advertising revenue exceeded company forecasts by fifteen percent.
Diversifying their offerings helped the firm maintain steady revenue despite the downturn.
memoryTip: From French 'revenir' (to return) — the money that returns to the business from sales.

meaning: a plan of action designed to achieve a long-term or overall aim
examples: Our digital growth strategy prioritizes customer retention over costly ad campaigns.
The executive board met in Geneva to formulate their five-year expansion strategy.
memoryTip: Originally a general's war plan (from Greek 'strategos') — your master plan to win.

meaning: as good as or better than others of a comparable nature; eager to succeed
examples: The retailer offers highly competitive prices without sacrificing product craftsmanship.
In a competitive job market, strong communication and technical skills set you apart.
memoryTip: Driven to compete and win against rival contenders.

meaning: to work jointly on an activity or project to produce or create something
examples: The two pharmaceutical labs chose to collaborate on developing an affordable vaccine.
Graphic designers and frontend developers must collaborate closely on user interfaces.
memoryTip: 'Co-' (together) + 'labor' (work) = working together.

meaning: a person, group, or organization with an interest or concern in something, especially a business
examples: The CEO scheduled town halls to address questions from every key corporate stakeholder.
Local community members are vital stakeholders in the coastal wind turbine project.
memoryTip: Holding a 'stake' (interest or investment) in the outcome of an enterprise.

meaning: to become or make larger or more extensive, especially a commercial operation
examples: The coffee chain plans to expand into three neighboring Southeast Asian nations.
They added five new warehouses to expand their nationwide logistics capacity.
memoryTip: Spread your wings out — expanding grows your footprint and reach.

meaning: a calculation or estimate of future events, especially coming weather or financial trends
examples: The chief financial officer presented an optimistic revenue forecast for the third quarter.
Supply chain forecasts help distributors stock sufficient inventory before holiday rushes.
memoryTip: 'Fore' (before) + 'cast' (throw) = throwing your vision forward into the future.

meaning: a risky or daring journey or an undertaking typically involving uncertainty and financial risk
examples: Their latest commercial venture into autonomous delivery drones attracted global investors.
Starting your own design agency is an exciting venture that requires resilience.
memoryTip: Think of an 'adventure' — an enterprise where you venture into unknown territory.

meaning: an asset or object bought or obtained, typically by a business buying another company
examples: The conglomerate finalized its billion-dollar acquisition of the cloud software firm.
Through strategic business acquisitions, the company rapidly entered foreign markets.
memoryTip: To 'acquire' something is to take ownership — acquisition is the finalized takeover.

meaning: an instance of buying or selling something; a business deal
examples: Contactless payment cards process the financial transaction in a fraction of a second.
All foreign exchange transactions are recorded in the central banking ledger.
memoryTip: 'Trans-' (across) + 'action' — an exchange of value taking place across two parties.

meaning: a person who organizes and operates a business or businesses, taking on greater than normal financial risks
examples: The young tech entrepreneur founded three profitable mobile apps before turning thirty.
Governments foster economic innovation by providing grants to aspiring entrepreneurs.
memoryTip: From French 'entreprendre' (to undertake) — someone who takes the risk to launch new ideas.

meaning: to wind up the affairs of a company or convert assets into readily spendable cash
examples: The bankrupt retail chain had to liquidate its warehouse inventory at huge discounts.
Investors chose to liquidate their shareholdings to raise cash during the market panic.
memoryTip: Turn solid assets (like buildings or machinery) into liquid cash.

meaning: the state or degree of being easily or conveniently done; practical viability
examples: Engineers conducted a detailed feasibility study before approving tunnel construction.
The feasibility of the mobile subscription model was proven by rising conversion rates.
memoryTip: Is it feasible? (Can it actually be done in the real world with available resources?)

meaning: the exclusive possession or control of the supply of or trade in a commodity or service
examples: Anti-trust regulators filed a lawsuit to break up the national railway monopoly.
Holding a patent gave the pharmaceutical company a temporary monopoly on the medicine.
memoryTip: 'Mono' means one — one single player controls the entire market board.

meaning: a number of different things or parts that are put or grouped together to form a whole, especially a large corporation
examples: The multinational media conglomerate owns newspaper networks, film studios, and streaming apps.
A family-owned conglomerate expanded its portfolio into shipping, real estate, and hotels.
memoryTip: Glomerate means clustered like a ball — a huge corporate cluster of diverse businesses.

meaning: suitcases or other bags in which to pack personal belongings for traveling
examples: Airline staff placed priority baggage tags on our checked-in luggage.
Traveling with only carry-on luggage makes navigating bustling terminals so much easier.
memoryTip: Think of what you 'lug' around when setting off on a long vacation.

meaning: an official government document certifying identity and citizenship, permitting travel abroad
examples: Keep your passport and boarding pass in a secure zipped pouch inside your jacket.
She needed to renew her biometric passport before flying to Paris for the conference.
memoryTip: A document that grants you permission to 'pass' through the international 'port'.

meaning: a certificate or token showing that a fare or admission fee has been paid
examples: He showed his electronic train ticket on his smartphone to the ticket collector.
Booking your flight tickets several weeks ahead can save hundreds of pounds.
memoryTip: A ticket gives you the green 'tick' to board the train or airplane.

meaning: a complex of runways and buildings for the takeoff, landing, and maintenance of civil aircraft
examples: We took the express metro line directly from the city center to the airport terminal.
Security checkpoints at international airports require electronics to be screened.
memoryTip: A port designed for air travel, just as a seaport serves ocean ships.

meaning: an act of traveling from one place to another, especially over a long distance
examples: The overnight train journey through the snow-covered mountains was breathtaking.
Learning a foreign language is a lifelong journey requiring patience and curiosity.
memoryTip: Originally meant a single 'day's travel' (from French 'journée' = day).

meaning: an establishment providing accommodation, meals, and other services for travelers and tourists
examples: Our boutique hotel in Rome was situated just a short stroll from the Colosseum.
The hotel concierge recommended a charming local trattoria for dinner.
memoryTip: Shares origins with 'hospitality' — a welcoming place to rest your head.

meaning: to go to see and spend time with someone socially or go to see a place as a tourist
examples: We took advantage of the sunny weekend to visit the ancient coastal fortress.
International tourists love to visit Kyoto during the spring cherry blossom season.
memoryTip: From Latin 'visere' (to look at or view) — seeing sights with your own eyes.

meaning: to reach a destination at the end of a journey or a stage of a journey
examples: Our flight is scheduled to arrive in London Heathrow at six tomorrow morning.
When you arrive at the hotel lobby, message me so we can meet for coffee.
memoryTip: Originally meant coming to shore ('ad ripam') — reaching the safe banks of your destination.

meaning: of, from, in, or characteristic of a country or language other than one's own
examples: Learning a foreign language broadens your worldview and enriches your travels.
Exchange students quickly adapt to the customs and cuisine of foreign cultures.
memoryTip: Related to 'outside' — originating outside your home borders.

meaning: to travel in or through an unfamiliar area in order to learn about it
examples: We spent three days renting bicycles to explore the historic alleyways of Seville.
Marine biologists dive into ocean trenches to explore unseen deep-sea habitats.
memoryTip: Step outside the beaten path to explore and make fresh discoveries.

meaning: a thing that is kept as a reminder of a person, place, or event
examples: I bought a miniature wooden windmill in Amsterdam as a travel souvenir.
Her travel shelf is adorned with handcrafted souvenirs collected from six continents.
memoryTip: From French 'se souvenir' (to remember) — a keepsake that sparks fond memories.

meaning: the place to which someone or something is going or being sent
examples: The Maldives remains one of the world's most sought-after honeymoon destinations.
After sixteen hours on the road, the exhausted hikers finally reached their destination.
memoryTip: Related to 'destiny' — the final end-point you are destined to reach.

meaning: a traveler on a public or private conveyance other than the driver, pilot, or crew
examples: The flight attendant instructed passengers to fasten their seatbelts before landing.
Subway stations in Tokyo handle millions of commuter passengers every weekday.
memoryTip: Someone passing along the journey under another person's steerage.

meaning: the action of leaving, especially to start a journey
examples: Check the departure monitor in the terminal to verify your flight's gate number.
Their early morning departure from port caught the rising sunrise across the bay.
memoryTip: To 'depart' is to leave — departure is your journey taking off.

meaning: to travel some distance between one's home and place of work on a regular basis
examples: Thousands of professionals commute into central London by suburban rail every day.
She uses her forty-minute morning commute to listen to educational audiobooks.
memoryTip: A daily recurring trip between home and work.

meaning: a planned route or journey, often with a detailed list of dates, times, and activities
examples: Our travel agent emailed a detailed 10-day itinerary for our tour across Scotland.
Leave some free afternoons in your holiday itinerary for spontaneous discoveries.
memoryTip: From Latin 'iter' (journey) — the step-by-step itinerary maps the journey.

meaning: an arrangement whereby something, especially a room or seat, is booked in advance
examples: I made a dinner reservation for four at the harbor seafood restaurant.
You will receive an instant confirmation code once your hotel reservation is processed.
memoryTip: A seat or room 'reserved' exclusively under your name.

meaning: a journey or voyage undertaken by a group of people with a particular purpose, especially exploration or research
examples: The scientific expedition collected ice core samples from glaciers in Antarctica.
Mountaineers spent six months preparing for their grueling expedition up K2.
memoryTip: Latin 'expedire' (to set free / go forth) — venturing on a daring trek.

meaning: friendly and welcoming to strangers or guests; having an environment where living is pleasant
examples: The islanders were incredibly hospitable, treating visitors to homecooked feasts.
A warm and hospitable atmosphere made the remote mountain guesthouse unforgettable.
memoryTip: Shares root with hospital and host — making a guest feel cared for and at home.

meaning: a strong, innate desire or impulse to wander or travel and explore the world
examples: Her incurable wanderlust led her to backpack solo across Southeast Asia for a year.
Looking through vintage travel magazines sparked an intense wanderlust inside him.
memoryTip: From German 'wandern' (wander) + 'lust' (desire) = a deep thirst to wander the globe.

meaning: visually attractive, especially in a quaint or charming style resembling a picture
examples: The train passed through picturesque fishing villages perched on dramatic cliffs.
Cobblestone streets and blooming balconies make this alpine town remarkably picturesque.
memoryTip: Picture-esque — so scenic and charming it looks like a painted postcard.

meaning: a period of rest or waiting between stages of a long journey, especially between flights
examples: We had a four-hour layover in Doha, allowing us to stretch and visit the airport garden.
Choosing a flight with an overnight layover can often reduce international airfares.
memoryTip: You 'lay over' between connecting flights while waiting for your next leg.

meaning: a journey to a place associated with someone or something well known or respected, often of moral or religious significance
examples: Every year, thousands of literature lovers make a pilgrimage to Shakespeare's birthplace.
Walking the Camino de Santiago is a traditional pilgrimage that spans northern Spain.
memoryTip: A pilgrim travels with reverence to an inspiring, historic, or holy destination.

meaning: the carrying of people or goods from one place to another; passage through an intermediate area
examples: International passengers in transit do not require a local visa if they stay in the airport.
The rapid transit train network transports over two million urban riders every morning.
memoryTip: 'Trans' means across — moving people across a city or country.

meaning: the process or activity of accurately ascertaining one's position and planning and following a route
examples: Modern satellite navigation systems calculate the fastest driving route in real time.
Early Polynesian sailors mastered celestial navigation by reading ocean swells and stars.
memoryTip: Latin 'navis' (ship) — steering a vessel or vehicle safely along its course.

meaning: feeling or showing pleasure, contentment, or joy
examples: The children were overjoyed and happy when the summer holidays finally began.
Hearing from an old school friend after years apart made her truly happy.
memoryTip: Good things 'happen' (same root) that lift your spirits into a happy state.

meaning: having a strong feeling of displeasure, annoyance, or hostility
examples: He felt angry when he discovered that his bicycle had been damaged overnight.
Taking deep breaths helped him cool off before responding in an angry tone.
memoryTip: Anger flares up like a sudden spark — take a breath before you speak.

meaning: easily agitated or alarmed; tending to be anxious or apprehensive
examples: She felt slightly nervous before walking onto the auditorium stage to give her speech.
His nervous tapping on the table showed how worried he was about the exam results.
memoryTip: Your physical 'nerves' tingle when adrenaline surges before a big challenge.

meaning: feeling deep pleasure or satisfaction as a result of one's own achievements or qualities
examples: Her parents were immensely proud when she graduated at the top of her class.
He took proud ownership of his hand-built wooden bookshelf in the living room.
memoryTip: Standing tall with your chin held high after accomplishing something worthy.

meaning: sad because one has no friends or company; isolated
examples: Moving to a foreign city alone made him feel lonely during his first month.
A warm telephone call from home cheered her up when she felt lonely.
memoryTip: 'Lone' means by oneself — feeling sorrowful in your solitary state.

meaning: to form one's features into an expression of pleasure, amusement, or friendliness
examples: She couldn't help but smile when she saw the puppy playing with the ball.
A warm, genuine smile immediately puts strangers and new classmates at ease.
memoryTip: Turn that frown upside down — a smile is a curve that sets everything straight.

meaning: to feel or cause to feel anxious or troubled about actual or potential problems
examples: Try not to worry about things you cannot control; focus on your immediate preparation.
Parents often worry when their teenagers drive on icy roads at night.
memoryTip: Worrying doesn't take away tomorrow's trouble, it only robs today's peace.

meaning: an unexpected or astonishing event, fact, or thing; the feeling caused by it
examples: Her colleagues threw a surprise farewell party in the rooftop lounge.
To our pleasant surprise, the rain stopped just as we arrived at the beach.
memoryTip: From French 'surprendre' (to overtake / catch unaware).

meaning: feeling or showing an appreciation of kindness; thankful
examples: I am deeply grateful to my mentor for guiding me through my university research.
The rescued hikers were intensely grateful to the helicopter mountain rescue crew.
memoryTip: Full of 'gratitude' — counting your blessings with a thankful heart.

meaning: feeling or showing certainty about something or trust in oneself
examples: Thorough preparation made her confident that she would ace the job interview.
He spoke in a calm, confident voice that reassured everyone in the boardroom.
memoryTip: Latin 'confidere' means to have full trust — having faith in your own preparation.

meaning: feeling or showing envy of someone or their achievements and advantages
examples: Instead of feeling jealous of your peers' accomplishments, let their hard work inspire you.
He felt a pang of jealous sadness when he saw his friend's new sports car.
memoryTip: The 'green-eyed monster' — focusing bitterly on what others possess.

meaning: experiencing worry, unease, or nervousness, typically about an imminent event or uncertain outcome
examples: Applicants often feel anxious while waiting for admissions decisions to arrive.
Deep breathing exercises helped soothe her anxious thoughts before takeoff.
memoryTip: Like the feeling of angst — a tightening sensation caused by anticipated trouble.

meaning: noticeably happy and optimistic; causing happiness by its nature or appearance
examples: Her cheerful greeting always brightened the spirits of everyone in the office.
The clinic painted the pediatric ward in cheerful shades of yellow and sky blue.
memoryTip: Full of 'cheer' — like a joyful cheer at a celebration.

meaning: a state of physical ease and freedom from pain or constraint; consolation in grief
examples: A warm mug of tea and a cozy blanket brought her instant comfort after a taxing day.
Friends gathered to offer words of comfort and solidarity during his bereavement.
memoryTip: Latin 'com-' (together) + 'fortis' (strong) — bringing strength to someone in distress.

meaning: feelings of pity and sorrow for someone else's misfortune
examples: We sent flowers and a handwritten card to express our deepest sympathy.
She listened to his troubles with sincere sympathy and offered a shoulder to lean on.
memoryTip: 'Sym-' (together) + 'pathos' (feeling) — feeling sorrow alongside another person.

meaning: feeling or expressing distress and annoyance, especially because of inability to change or achieve something
examples: The programmer felt frustrated after hunting down a subtle bug for four hours.
Delays at the airport left hundreds of frustrated travelers stranded overnight.
memoryTip: When obstacles 'frustrate' your plans, irritation builds up inside.

meaning: having a strong emotional response; burdened by an excessive amount of something to deal with
examples: With five deadlines falling on the same Friday, the student felt completely overwhelmed.
She was emotionally overwhelmed by the outpouring of love at her retirement dinner.
memoryTip: Picture high waves surging over a boat — feeling submerged under too much weight.

meaning: feeling or expressing overwhelming happiness or joyful excitement
examples: The football fans were ecstatic when their team scored the winning goal in stoppage time.
She was ecstatic upon opening the envelope and finding her scholarship acceptance letter.
memoryTip: Full of 'ecstasy' — joy so intense you feel like dancing on clouds.

meaning: feeling or expressing pensive, deep, and gentle sadness
examples: The cello melody had a beautifully melancholic quality that moved the audience.
Watching autumn leaves drift down from the trees put her in a melancholic reverie.
memoryTip: A sweet, reflective sadness — like listening to rain outside your window.

meaning: the state of being calm, peaceful, and untroubled
examples: Walking along the misty lakeshore at dawn filled him with profound serenity.
Meditation and mindful breathing cultivate an inner serenity amidst chaotic workdays.
memoryTip: From 'serene' — like a clear, cloudless sky without a ripple on the water.

meaning: bitter indignation at having been treated unfairly
examples: Harboring hidden resentment over past grievances will poison any working relationship.
He felt a lingering resentment when a colleague took credit for his analytical model.
memoryTip: 'Re-sent' (feeling the sting repeatedly) — re-feeling an old hurt like bitter poison.

meaning: sympathetic pity and concern for the sufferings or misfortunes of others, accompanied by a desire to help
examples: Nurses in the pediatric ward treat their patients with boundless patience and compassion.
Genuine compassion moves beyond mere sympathy and takes active steps to relieve distress.
memoryTip: Latin 'compati' (to suffer with) — suffering with someone and reaching out to heal.

meaning: anxious or fearful that something bad or unpleasant will happen
examples: He felt deeply apprehensive as the surgeon approached with the biopsy results.
First-time drivers are often apprehensive when merging onto high-speed motorways.
memoryTip: You feel like trouble is about to reach out and apprehend (catch) you.

meaning: a sentimental longing or wistful affection for the past, typically for a period with happy personal associations
examples: Flipping through childhood photograph albums sparked a bittersweet wave of nostalgia.
The vinyl record store trades on nostalgia for classic music from the seventies.
memoryTip: Greek 'nostos' (homecoming) + 'algos' (pain) — the sweet ache of remembering home.

meaning: the ability to understand and share the feelings of another from their perspective
examples: Practicing empathy allows doctors to understand what a vulnerable patient is experiencing.
Great novelists possess the profound empathy needed to bring diverse characters to life.
memoryTip: Walking in another person's shoes — feeling what is inside ('em') their heart.

meaning: An electronic device that processes data and performs tasks according to instructions.
examples: She uses her computer to write assignments and research topics for class.
The office bought new computers to handle the growing workload efficiently.
memoryTip: Think of 'compute' + '-er': a device that computes (calculates) things.

meaning: A device used to send and receive calls, messages, and data, especially a smartphone.
examples: He forgot his phone at home and missed all the important notifications.
My phone's battery died just before I could board the train.
memoryTip: From Greek 'phonē' meaning 'voice' — a device for carrying your voice.

meaning: The flat display surface of a device such as a phone, computer, or television.
examples: She cracked her phone screen when it slipped out of her hand.
The professor projected the slides onto a large screen at the front of the lecture hall.
memoryTip: A screen is what you 'see' — it screens (shows) information to you.

meaning: A container that stores electrical energy and powers a device.
examples: Always charge your laptop battery before a long flight.
The smartwatch's battery lasts about two days on a single charge.
memoryTip: Think of a 'battery' as a 'store' of electricity — like a water tank for power.

meaning: A global network connecting millions of computers and devices to share information.
examples: Without internet access, she could not submit her assignment online.
The internet has made it possible to communicate with anyone around the world instantly.
memoryTip: 'Inter' (between) + 'net' (network): a network connecting networks.

meaning: To press a button on a mouse or tap an element on a touchscreen to perform an action.
examples: Click the button to save your document before closing the program.
She clicked on the link and was redirected to the payment page.
memoryTip: The word mimics the sound of pressing a mouse button — click!

meaning: To supply electrical energy to a battery or device so it can operate.
examples: He plugged his phone in to charge it overnight before the trip.
Make sure to fully charge your camera before the event starts.
memoryTip: To 'charge' a device is to load it with energy — like charging a weapon.

meaning: To look through data or the internet to find specific information.
examples: She searched online for tutorials on how to use the new software.
You can search the database by entering keywords in the search bar.
memoryTip: To 'search' is to seek — think of a search engine like a digital detective.

meaning: A system of connected computers or devices that can communicate and share resources.
examples: The company's internal network allows employees to share files securely.
His phone automatically connected to the university Wi-Fi network on campus.
memoryTip: A 'net' of 'work' — an interconnected web of devices doing work together.

meaning: A piece of electronic equipment designed to perform a specific function.
examples: He carried three devices — a phone, a tablet, and a laptop — to the conference.
Smart home devices allow you to control your lights and thermostat remotely.
memoryTip: A 'device' is a tool devised (invented) for a specific purpose.

meaning: Using radio waves instead of physical cables to transmit data or power.
examples: The wireless headphones connect to the phone using Bluetooth.
Most modern offices are set up with wireless internet to avoid cable clutter.
memoryTip: Literally 'without wire' — no cables needed for wireless connections.

meaning: Programs and operating systems that run on a computer or device.
examples: The latest software update fixed several bugs in the application.
She downloaded editing software to create short videos for her class project.
memoryTip: 'Soft' as in not physical: software is the intangible instructions, unlike 'hardware' you can touch.

meaning: The capacity of a device to hold data, files, and applications.
examples: Her phone's storage was full, so she deleted old photos to free up space.
Cloud storage lets you save files online and access them from any device.
memoryTip: Storage 'stores' data — think of it as a digital warehouse.

meaning: Protected against unauthorized access, threats, or risks.
examples: Always use a secure password that combines letters, numbers, and symbols.
The app stores your personal data on secure servers with end-to-end encryption.
memoryTip: Think of a 'secure' lock — it keeps data locked away from intruders.

meaning: To transfer data from a server or the internet to your local device.
examples: He downloaded the app from the official store onto his phone.
It took only a few seconds to download the PDF file on the high-speed connection.
memoryTip: Think of data flowing 'down' from the internet into your device.

meaning: The process of converting data into a coded format to prevent unauthorized access.
examples: End-to-end encryption ensures that only the sender and receiver can read the messages.
The company uses strong encryption to protect customers' payment details.
memoryTip: Think of 'en-crypt' — putting data in a crypt (hidden underground vault).

meaning: The point of interaction between a user and a computer system, often visual.
examples: The app's clean interface makes it easy for beginners to navigate without confusion.
The designer improved the user interface so customers could find products more quickly.
memoryTip: 'Inter' (between) + 'face': the face between you and the machine.

meaning: An organized collection of structured data stored and accessed electronically.
examples: The hospital maintains a database of all patient records and treatment histories.
She searched the university's database to find previous research papers on the topic.
memoryTip: A 'database' is the 'base' or foundation where all your 'data' lives.

meaning: A set of step-by-step instructions that a computer follows to solve a problem.
examples: Social media platforms use algorithms to decide which posts appear in your feed.
The sorting algorithm arranged the list of names in alphabetical order within seconds.
memoryTip: Named after mathematician Al-Khwarizmi — a recipe of steps for the computer to follow.

meaning: Able to work together or be used together without conflict.
examples: Make sure the charger is compatible with your phone before using it.
The software is compatible with both Windows and Mac operating systems.
memoryTip: Think of 'compat' (compact/together) — devices that fit together are compatible.

meaning: To make a process operate automatically without manual human input.
examples: The factory automated its assembly line to increase production speed.
She used a script to automate the repetitive task of renaming hundreds of files.
memoryTip: Auto = self: to automate is to make something run 'by itself' automatically.

meaning: The amount of data that can be transmitted over a network connection per unit of time.
examples: Streaming high-quality video requires a lot of bandwidth.
During peak hours, shared bandwidth can slow down everyone's internet speed.
memoryTip: Think of a 'band' (pipe) — wider bandwidth means a bigger pipe for more data to flow through.

meaning: Made or produced by humans rather than occurring naturally; not real.
examples: Artificial intelligence systems can now generate realistic images from text descriptions.
The lab used artificial light to simulate daylight conditions for the experiment.
memoryTip: Think of 'artifact' — something made by human artistry, not nature.

meaning: To cause two or more systems or devices to operate at the same time or match the same data.
examples: The app synchronizes your contacts across all your devices automatically.
He synchronized his calendar on his phone with the one on his laptop.
memoryTip: 'Syn' (together) + 'chronos' (time): happening at the same time.

meaning: The process of verifying the identity of a user or device before granting access.
examples: Two-factor authentication adds an extra layer of security beyond just a password.
Biometric authentication uses fingerprints or facial recognition to verify identity.
memoryTip: Think of 'authentic' — authentication checks if you are genuinely who you claim to be.

meaning: A tall perennial plant with a woody trunk, branches, and leaves.
examples: The old mango tree in the garden provides shade during the hot summer months.
They planted a new tree in the park every year on World Environment Day.
memoryTip: Trees 'stand tall' — think of them as the skyscrapers of the natural world.

meaning: A large natural stream of water flowing toward a sea, lake, or another river.
examples: The children played near the river bank, watching fish swim below the surface.
Heavy rainfall caused the river to flood the nearby villages overnight.
memoryTip: Think of a river 'running' — rivers are nature's constantly moving highways.

meaning: A visible mass of water droplets or ice crystals suspended in the atmosphere.
examples: Dark clouds gathered on the horizon, warning of an approaching storm.
She lay on the grass, watching fluffy clouds drift lazily across the blue sky.
memoryTip: Clouds 'float' in the sky — the word comes from Old English 'clud' meaning rock or hill.

meaning: The colourful, often fragrant part of a plant that attracts pollinators.
examples: She picked a bouquet of wild flowers from the meadow for the dinner table.
The cherry flowers bloom beautifully every spring, turning the trees pink.
memoryTip: A flower 'flowers' (blooms) — the verb and noun share the same root.

meaning: A large area of land covered with trees and undergrowth.
examples: They hiked through the dense forest for hours before reaching the waterfall.
Tropical rainforests are home to more than half of the world's plant and animal species.
memoryTip: A forest is full of trees — 'forest' comes from Latin 'forestis' meaning 'outside' (the forest was outside the town).

meaning: The area where land meets the sea; the shoreline and its surrounding region.
examples: They spent the weekend at the coast, swimming in the sea and walking on the beach.
Many fishing villages are found along the southern coast of the island.
memoryTip: The coast is where land 'coasts' into the sea — the meeting point of two worlds.

meaning: The atmospheric conditions at a particular place and time, such as temperature, rain, and wind.
examples: The weather forecast predicted heavy showers throughout the afternoon.
She always checks the weather before planning an outdoor event.
memoryTip: Think of 'whether' — weather makes you wonder 'whether' to bring an umbrella.

meaning: To keep safe from harm, damage, or destruction.
examples: National parks were created to protect rare animals and plants from human interference.
We must protect our water sources by reducing industrial pollution near rivers.
memoryTip: Pro + tect: 'pro' (for) + 'tegere' (to cover) — to cover or shield something for safety.

meaning: Animals, birds, and other living organisms that live in natural environments.
examples: The national reserve is home to diverse wildlife including leopards and elephants.
Urban expansion threatens wildlife by destroying their natural habitats.
memoryTip: Wildlife = wild + life: creatures living wild, in their natural state.

meaning: The natural environment in which a plant or animal lives and grows.
examples: Coral reefs are the natural habitat of thousands of marine species.
Deforestation is destroying the habitat of orangutans in Borneo.
memoryTip: Think of 'inhabit' — a habitat is the place an animal inhabits (lives in).

meaning: The long-term pattern of weather conditions in a specific region.
examples: Sri Lanka has a tropical climate with high humidity and regular rainfall.
Scientists are studying how climate change will affect crop production in the future.
memoryTip: Climate = long-term weather. Weather changes daily; climate changes over decades.

meaning: To protect and preserve natural resources, wildlife, or the environment.
examples: Turning off lights when leaving a room helps conserve energy.
The government launched a campaign to conserve the country's endangered coral reefs.
memoryTip: Think of 'conservation' — to conserve is to keep something from disappearing.

meaning: A group of living organisms that share common characteristics and can interbreed.
examples: Scientists have discovered hundreds of new plant species in the Amazon rainforest.
The blue whale is the largest species of animal on Earth.
memoryTip: Species comes from Latin 'specere' (to look at) — a category defined by appearance and traits.

meaning: The introduction of harmful substances into the natural environment.
examples: Air pollution from vehicle emissions is a serious health concern in many cities.
Plastic pollution in the ocean kills millions of marine animals every year.
memoryTip: Think of 'pollute' — pollution 'pollutes' (dirties) the clean environment.

meaning: Describing a natural resource that is replenished naturally and will not run out.
examples: Solar and wind are renewable energy sources that do not produce harmful emissions.
Switching to renewable energy is one of the most effective ways to fight climate change.
memoryTip: Re + new + able: something that can be made 'new' again repeatedly.

meaning: A community of living organisms interacting with each other and their physical environment.
examples: The destruction of a single species can disrupt an entire ecosystem.
Coral reefs represent one of the most diverse and complex ecosystems on the planet.
memoryTip: 'Eco' (home/environment) + 'system': the system of life in a natural home.

meaning: The variety of plant and animal life in a particular habitat or on Earth.
examples: Tropical rainforests have incredible biodiversity, sheltering millions of species.
Protecting biodiversity is essential for maintaining healthy ecosystems and food chains.
memoryTip: 'Bio' (life) + 'diversity' (variety): the variety of life forms sharing our planet.

meaning: The gradual wearing away of rock or soil by natural forces such as wind, water, or ice.
examples: Coastal erosion is slowly shrinking the beach near the town.
Planting trees on bare hillsides helps prevent soil erosion during heavy rainfall.
memoryTip: Think of 'erode' — water erodes rocks gradually, like time 'eats away' at them.

meaning: Able to continue over a long period without damaging the natural environment.
examples: Sustainable farming practices protect soil health for future generations.
She chose a sustainable brand that uses recycled materials in its packaging.
memoryTip: Think of 'sustain' — sustainable means you can sustain (keep going) without harming nature.

meaning: A prolonged period of abnormally low rainfall, leading to water shortage.
examples: The severe drought caused crop failures and food shortages across the region.
Water reservoirs fell to record lows after three years of drought.
memoryTip: Drought rhymes with 'out' — the water is 'out' (gone) during a drought.

meaning: Any living thing, including plants, animals, fungi, and microorganisms.
examples: Even tiny organisms like bacteria play an important role in breaking down organic matter.
The ocean is home to organisms ranging from microscopic plankton to giant whales.
memoryTip: Think of 'organ' — an organism is an 'organized' living system with working organs.

meaning: The protection and careful management of natural resources and wildlife.
examples: Wildlife conservation efforts have helped the tiger population recover in some regions.
Water conservation is especially important during the dry season.
memoryTip: Conservation = 'conserving' nature: keeping it safe for the future.

meaning: A change in an organism that makes it better suited to its environment over time.
examples: The camel's ability to store water is an adaptation for surviving in the desert.
Over thousands of years, polar bears developed adaptations to live in freezing temperatures.
memoryTip: To 'adapt' is to change to fit — adaptation is nature's way of solving survival problems.

meaning: The process by which plants use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to produce food and oxygen.
examples: Without photosynthesis, plants could not produce the oxygen that all animals breathe.
During our biology lesson, we learned how leaves use chlorophyll for photosynthesis.
memoryTip: 'Photo' (light) + 'synthesis' (making): plants making food from light.

meaning: The process of replanting trees in areas where forests have been cut down or destroyed.
examples: The government launched a reforestation programme to restore deforested hillsides.
Reforestation helps reduce carbon dioxide in the atmosphere and restore wildlife habitats.
memoryTip: 'Re' (again) + 'forestation' (planting forests): planting forests again where they were lost.

meaning: A clear, odourless liquid essential for all living things; H₂O.
examples: Doctors recommend drinking at least eight glasses of water every day.
After the long run, she was exhausted and needed water to stay hydrated.
memoryTip: Water = life. The human body is about 60% water — it is the most essential nutrient.

meaning: A naturally recurring state of rest for the mind and body, essential for health.
examples: Getting at least seven hours of sleep each night improves concentration and mood.
He felt exhausted all week because stress was disrupting his sleep.
memoryTip: Think of sleep as your body's 'reboot' — just like a computer needs a restart, so does your brain.

meaning: Physical activity done to improve health and maintain fitness.
examples: Regular exercise helps reduce the risk of heart disease and diabetes.
She goes for a 30-minute walk every morning as part of her daily exercise routine.
memoryTip: Exercise 'exerts' your body — think of it as putting your muscles to work.

meaning: Having or showing good physical and mental wellbeing.
examples: Eating a healthy diet with plenty of vegetables and fruit improves your energy levels.
The doctor confirmed that her blood pressure was in the healthy range.
memoryTip: Think of 'health' + '-y': something that contributes to or shows good health.

meaning: The physical and mental strength needed to perform activities and stay alert.
examples: She didn't have enough energy to finish her assignment after skipping lunch.
A balanced breakfast gives your body the energy it needs to get through the morning.
memoryTip: Energy comes from Greek 'energeia' (activity) — the fuel that keeps you active.

meaning: A period of relaxation or inactivity to recover strength and energy.
examples: The doctor advised her to take two days of complete rest after the minor surgery.
Even on busy days, taking a short rest in the afternoon improves afternoon productivity.
memoryTip: Think of 'rest' as your body pressing 'pause' — it restores what effort uses up.

meaning: A substance used to treat or prevent illness, or the science of diagnosing and treating disease.
examples: She took her medicine exactly as the doctor prescribed, twice a day after meals.
He is studying medicine at university and hopes to become a paediatrician.
memoryTip: Think of 'medic' — medicine is what a medic uses to heal you.

meaning: A sign or indication of a disease or health problem experienced by a patient.
examples: Common symptoms of the flu include fever, headache, and muscle aches.
She visited the clinic as soon as she noticed symptoms of an ear infection.
memoryTip: A symptom 'signals' a problem — it is your body's way of sending a message.

meaning: To take air into the lungs and release it, sustaining life.
examples: During meditation, focus on how you breathe — slow, deep breaths calm the mind.
It was difficult to breathe properly at high altitudes due to the thin air.
memoryTip: Notice 'breathe' has an 'e' at the end — that's the verb. 'Breath' (no 'e') is the noun.

meaning: A person receiving medical treatment or care from a healthcare professional.
examples: The doctor spent extra time with each patient to explain their diagnosis clearly.
As a patient, you have the right to ask questions about your treatment options.
memoryTip: A patient must often be 'patient' (adjective: calm and waiting) while receiving care.

meaning: A state of physical or mental stability; having the right proportions of different elements.
examples: Maintaining a healthy work-life balance is important for long-term wellbeing.
A balanced diet includes carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, and minerals.
memoryTip: Picture a weighing scale — balance means both sides are equal, nothing is too much or too little.

meaning: The process of obtaining food needed for health and growth.
examples: Good nutrition during childhood is essential for healthy brain and body development.
She studied nutrition to understand how different foods affect the body.
memoryTip: Think of 'nutrient' — nutrition is about getting the right nutrients into your body.

meaning: To return to a normal state of health after illness or injury.
examples: It took her two weeks to fully recover from the flu.
With plenty of rest and good nutrition, most patients recover quickly from minor surgery.
memoryTip: Re + cover: to 're-cover' yourself — getting back the health that illness took away.

meaning: To stop something, especially illness or harm, from happening.
examples: Washing your hands regularly is one of the simplest ways to prevent the spread of germs.
Wearing sunscreen can prevent skin damage caused by harmful UV rays.
memoryTip: 'Pre' (before) + 'vent': to stop something before it even starts.

meaning: The process of supplying adequate water to the body to maintain proper function.
examples: Proper hydration is crucial during exercise to avoid cramps and dizziness.
He kept a water bottle at his desk to remind himself to maintain good hydration throughout the day.
memoryTip: 'Hydro' means water in Greek — hydration is keeping your body full of water.

meaning: Protected against or resistant to a particular disease or infection.
examples: After recovering from chickenpox, the body becomes immune to future infections.
Vaccines help people become immune to serious diseases without having to get sick first.
memoryTip: Think of your immune system as your personal army — it fights off invading germs.

meaning: The active pursuit of activities and choices that lead to holistic health.
examples: Many companies now offer wellness programmes to support employees' mental health.
Wellness is not just the absence of illness — it also includes emotional and social wellbeing.
memoryTip: Wellness = well + ness: the state of being 'well' in every area of life.

meaning: To identify the nature of a disease or condition by examining symptoms.
examples: The doctor was able to diagnose the infection from the blood test results.
It can be difficult to diagnose mental health conditions without a thorough assessment.
memoryTip: 'Dia' (through) + 'gnosis' (knowledge): gaining knowledge through thorough examination.

meaning: Treatment intended to relieve or cure a disorder, whether physical or mental.
examples: She began attending weekly therapy sessions to manage anxiety.
Physical therapy helped him regain strength in his knee after the surgery.
memoryTip: Think of 'therapeutic' — therapy is any treatment that makes you feel better.

meaning: Describing an illness or condition that lasts a long time or recurs persistently.
examples: She lives with chronic back pain that affects her ability to sit for long periods.
Chronic stress can lead to serious health problems including high blood pressure.
memoryTip: 'Chrono' means time — a chronic condition is one that stays with you over a long time.

meaning: An official written instruction by a doctor authorising a patient to receive medicine.
examples: The pharmacist asked for a prescription before dispensing the antibiotics.
She kept all her prescriptions organised in a folder for reference during check-ups.
memoryTip: 'Pre' (before) + 'scription' (writing): written instructions prepared before you receive medicine.

meaning: The process of restoring someone to full health and normal life after illness or injury.
examples: After the stroke, the patient underwent rehabilitation to relearn basic motor skills.
Sports rehabilitation helps athletes recover safely and return to peak performance.
memoryTip: 'Re' (again) + 'habilitate' (make able): making someone capable again after illness.

meaning: Designed to stop disease or harm before it occurs.
examples: Annual health checks are a preventive measure to catch problems early.
The government invested in preventive healthcare to reduce hospital admissions.
memoryTip: Think 'prevent' + '-ive': preventive care acts before an illness can take hold.

meaning: The chemical processes in the body that convert food into energy.
examples: Regular exercise can boost your metabolism, helping you burn calories more efficiently.
Some people have a naturally faster metabolism, which affects how quickly they digest food.
memoryTip: 'Meta' (change) + 'bole' (throwing): metabolism 'throws' your food into energy through chemical changes.

meaning: A person's overall health, happiness, and comfort — physical, mental, and social.
examples: Looking after your mental well-being is just as important as physical health.
The school introduced mindfulness classes to support students' emotional well-being.
memoryTip: Well + being: the state of 'being well' in all aspects — body, mind, and spirit.
